title: A 404 page that keeps the visit
metaTitle: A 404 page that keeps the visit
excerpt: Say the page is gone, then offer the homepage and the one action. A joke that hides those two paths wastes a visit you already earned.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp. The quiet workspace fits a page about recovering a visit after a missing URL.
caption: The missing page still needs a clear next step. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a 404 page say?
faqs.answer: Say that this address does not lead to a page, in plain language. Then offer the homepage and the single action you most want a stranger to take, such as booking a call or viewing the work. A joke can sit in a small line beside that. It cannot replace it.

faqs.question: Should every missing URL redirect to the homepage?
faqs.answer: No. A person who followed a link to a pricing page, a product, or an old article needs to know that specific page is gone. Dropping them on the homepage hides the failure and makes them start the search again. Keep a real not-found page, and redirect only the URLs you retired on purpose.

faqs.question: How many links belong on a 404 page?
faqs.answer: Two is enough: home, and the one action. A search box helps if the site is large and the search actually works. A grid of every page on the site turns the error into a sitemap. Nielsen Norman Group's research on page visits is a reminder that people decide quickly, so the useful paths have to be visible at once.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A missing address should tell the truth and offer a way forward. That is the whole of 404 page design. Say the page is gone. Put the homepage and the one action you care about where a person can see them without hunting.

People land here from an old bookmark, a shared link, a campaign that outlived its URL, or a result that still points at a page you renamed. They already decided to visit. The error page either returns them to the site or spends that decision on a joke they have to decode.

## Say what happened

Write one sentence a stranger can repeat. "This page does not exist" is enough. "We looked everywhere and the page wandered off" makes the reader do extra work before they know the facts. The status is an error. The copy can be calm. It does not need to be cute to be human.

Name the situation, not the server. Most visitors do not know what 404 means, and the ones who do still want the next step. You can show the code in small type for the person who is debugging a link. The headline is for the person who wanted the page.

If you retired the page on purpose, say that when you know it. "This offer has closed" is different from "we cannot find this address." A founder who merged two products, or took a role off the careers list, should not pretend the URL was a typo. The honest sentence is shorter than the apology.

Keep the same voice you use on the rest of the site. A 404 is still your site. A sudden change into a cartoon, a different logo, or a template from the host is a second surprise on top of the first. The header, the type, and the footer should match. The message is the only thing that should feel specific to this moment.

## Two ways forward

Offer the homepage and the one action. For a studio or a young company, the action is usually the intro call, the work, or the product. Pick the one a lost visitor can use. A row of eight equal links is a second navigation problem at the worst moment.

The homepage link should say "homepage" or the name of the company, so the destination is obvious. The action link should say what they get. "Book a 30-minute intro" is a destination. "Click here" is not. If the site is a store, the second link might be the shop, not a newsletter. Match the link to the reason people come.

A search field is a third option only when search works and the site is large enough that people cannot guess the URL. On a ten-page marketing site, search is furniture. On a journal or a catalog, it is a real recovery tool. If you include it, put it under the two links, not instead of them.

Do not auto-redirect every unknown URL to the homepage. The person who typed a product name, or followed a link to a case study, needs to see that the specific page failed. A silent redirect feels like the site ignored them. It also makes broken links harder for you to notice, because the error never shows itself. Redirect the URLs you moved, with a proper permanent redirect, and let the rest fall through to this page.

## The joke that hides the path

A small aside is fine. A full-screen illustration with no sentence, or a puzzle the visitor must solve to find the menu, spends the visit on the studio's sense of humor. The person did not come for the error. They came for a page. If the joke is the largest thing on the screen, the path has disappeared.

Nielsen Norman Group's summary of page-visit research is blunt about the clock. Users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are when they decide whether the page is worth more time. To earn a longer look, the value has to be clear inside that window. A 404 has even less goodwill than a homepage. The value here is the way back. If that way back is under a punchline, you are asking for a second decision they may not make.

Humor also dates. A reference that landed in a pitch meeting is noise to a buyer six months later, and it is noise to anyone outside the team. Read the line out loud to someone who does not work with you. If they smile and then ask where to go, the joke is too big. If they can say the next step without help, the joke is in its place.

Keep the illustration, if you want one, in the role of a picture, not a riddle. A quiet image from the same world as the rest of the site is enough. The caption or the adjacent sentence still has to say the page is gone and where to go next. Decorative work that needs a paragraph of explanation has failed the job.

## What to keep from the rest of the site

Use the real header. A lost visitor who can still see Products, Work, or Book a call may never need the body of the 404. Stripping the navigation to "be minimal" removes the tools they already know. The error page is a page in the system, not a poster.

Use the real footer too, including the short legal links and the contact line. Someone whose link broke may have been trying to reach you. A 404 with no way to write, and no way home, is a closed door. You do not need a new contact form on the error. You need the one you already trust.

Match the focus order a keyboard user expects. The skip link, the logo, the primary action, then the two recovery links. A giant animated scene that traps focus, or a canvas that cannot be tabbed past, turns a wrong URL into an access problem. The page is short. It can be correct.

If the site has a client portal or a signed-in area, do not send anonymous traffic toward it from the 404. Offer the public next step. A login wall as the recovery path punishes someone who followed an old public link.

## Broken links you can prevent

The best 404 is the one fewer people see. When you rename a page, redirect the old URL. When you unpublish a case study, decide whether the URL should explain the removal or point at the work index. When a campaign ends, leave the landing page up with a current sentence, or redirect it, rather than deleting it the day the ads stop.

Keep a short list of URLs that matter: the homepage, the offer, the work, the booking link, and any page a partner has in print. Check them when you launch. A redesign that changes slugs without redirects will fill the 404 with your own audience. That is the expensive version of this page.

Watch the not-found log after launch, even if you only glance once a week. Repeated hits on one path mean a link in the wild is wrong: a footer, a partner site, an old newsletter, a PDF. Fix the link or add the redirect. A clever 404 that stays busy is a sign the site is leaking, not a sign the error page is a success.

On a Hanabi build, the marketing pages are ordinary routes in the repository, so a renamed page is a redirect we can write down beside the page, not a setting buried in a plugin. The 404 is a designed template with the same header as the rest of the site. The habit is the point. The error page stays boring on purpose, and the redirects do the real recovery.

## A check before you ship it

Read the page on a phone, with the keyboard closed. You should see the sentence, the homepage, and the action without scrolling past a drawing. Tap both links. They should go where the words say. Then tab from the top of the page on a desktop browser. You should reach those same two links in a sensible order.

Ask someone outside the company to open a URL you know is wrong. Do not explain. Watch whether they can say, in one sentence, what happened and what they would do next. If they describe the illustration and then go quiet, the path is too quiet.

Set the status code to a real not-found response so browsers and monitors can tell the error from a normal page. A page that looks like an error but returns a success code will be cached, measured, and sometimes indexed as if it were content. The copy and the code should agree.

Leave the page out of your primary navigation. Nobody should be invited to the error. It is a landing place for accidents, and it should be ready for them. Once it is ready, stop decorating it. The next hour is better spent on the links that send people there.

If a missing page is part of a larger site that needs a calmer structure, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) to see how public projects hold a visitor on the pages that do exist. The error page is the spare path. The work is the reason to take it.

When the page does load and then sits on gray boxes, the visit fails in a different way. [Loading and skeletons on a marketing site](/blog/loading-and-skeletons-on-a-marketing-site) is the next piece, because a placeholder is the other way a page asks someone to wait for the thing they came to read.
